content.text:
Prompt Interpretation:
- You want an evidence-based evaluation of whether Keir Starmer values human rights, backed by sources I look up now.
- You also want a per-URL digest (link, what it says, whether it’s trusted, and why), plus a short account of my method and any assumptions before I conclude.

Reasoning Process:
- I operationalised “values human rights” as: (a) consistent, recent commitments to cornerstone human-rights frameworks (e.g., the European Convention on Human Rights, Human Rights Act), (b) concrete government actions that advance rights/accountability, and (c) a track record of human-rights advocacy in his legal career.
- I prioritised primary sources (official speeches/transcripts, Hansard, government papers, Parliament Library briefings) and reputable institutions, then added high‑quality secondary reporting where useful. I verified dates (2013–2025) and favoured sources published during Starmer’s premiership (since 5 July 2024) to show current stance.
- I included one or two items evidencing nuance (e.g., proposals to revisit interpretation of some ECHR articles) to present an honest picture while still assessing whether he “values” human rights overall.

Assumptions:
- “Values human rights” means demonstrable commitment in words and deeds to protect and uphold human rights and the rule of law; it does not require never balancing rights with other policy aims (e.g., immigration control).
- Government statements from ministers and official platforms represent Starmer’s government policy unless contradicted.
- A long human‑rights legal career indicates genuine commitment, especially when corroborated by independent institutions.

Final Answer:
Below are the sources I found and relied upon. For each, I include URL, a concise summary, my trust assessment, and why.

1) URL: PM speech to the INTERPOL General Assembly: 4 November 2024 (GOV.UK)
- Summary: Starmer states “We will never withdraw from the European Convention on Human Rights,” situating UK security policy as “rooted in our values… respect for human rights and upholding the rule of law.” Emphasises treating people‑smuggling as organised crime while operating within international law. 
- Trust: TRUSTED
- Reasoning: Primary source, official government transcript with exact wording and date. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/pm-speech-to-the-interpol-general-assembly-4-november-2024?utm_source=openai))

2) URL: Hansard (Lords), 7 January 2025 — ECHR 75th Anniversary
- Summary: Government minister (MoJ) states the Starmer government “will never withdraw from the ECHR,” reaffirming commitment to the international human‑rights framework. 
- Trust: TRUSTED
- Reasoning: Official parliamentary record; authoritative and dated. ([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/Lords/2025-01-07/debates/9276ABB4-7B70-4A5B-80BE-BEE90DA891AF/EuropeanConventionOnHumanRights75ThAnniversary?utm_source=openai))

3) URL: Hansard (Lords), 17 July 2025 — European Convention on Human Rights
- Summary: Minister restates that the government is “fully committed” to domestic and international human‑rights protection and to constructive dialogue within the ECHR framework (i.e., engagement, not exit). 
- Trust: TRUSTED
- Reasoning: Official parliamentary record; confirms continuity of policy mid‑2025. ([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/lords/2025-07-17/debates/E4614651-E5AF-4A48-814B-46451642A875/EuropeanConventionOnHumanRights?utm_source=openai))

4) URL: Labour Party policy page (Scotland – “A strong and connected country”)
- Summary: States Labour “values international law” and the UK will “unequivocally remain a member of the European Convention on Human Rights.” 
- Trust: TRUSTED (with partisan‑source caveat)
- Reasoning: Official party statement; partisan but consistent with government line and primary sources. ([labour.org.uk](https://labour.org.uk/change/scotland-a-strong-and-connected-country/?utm_source=openai))

5) URL: Hillsborough Law press release (GOV.UK), 15 September 2025
- Summary: Government introduces “Hillsborough Law” to impose a legal duty of candour on public authorities, expand legal aid for bereaved families at inquests, and create offences for misleading the public—aimed at transparency, accountability, and justice for victims. 
- Trust: TRUSTED
- Reasoning: Primary source announcing a rights‑advancing measure focused on victims’ access to justice and state accountability. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/hillsborough-law-to-ensure-truth-never-concealed-by-state-again?utm_source=openai))

6) URL: Hillsborough Law policy paper (GOV.UK), 16 September 2025
- Summary: Official policy paper for the Public Office (Accountability) Bill, detailing the duty of candour, “parity of arms” for bereaved families, and reforms to misconduct in public office. 
- Trust: TRUSTED
- Reasoning: Primary government documentation of substantive legislative steps tied to accountability rights. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/hillsborough-law-bill?utm_source=openai))

7) URL: Public Office (Accountability) Bill — House of Commons Library briefing
- Summary: Neutral briefing explains the Bill (widely called “Hillsborough Law”), its purpose (candour duty, parity of representation, new offences), and legislative context. 
- Trust: TRUSTED
- Reasoning: Independent, non‑partisan parliamentary research; corroborates scope and intent. ([commonslibrary.parliament.uk](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-10359/?utm_source=openai))

8) URL: Public Office (Accountability) Bill — Parliamentary Bills page
- Summary: Confirms the Bill’s long title, scope, and introduction date (16 Sept 2025), showing legislative follow‑through. 
- Trust: TRUSTED
- Reasoning: Primary legislative tracking from UK Parliament. ([bills.parliament.uk](https://bills.parliament.uk/bills/4019?utm_source=openai))

9) URL: St Edmund Hall, University of Oxford — Honorary Fellow profile
- Summary: Details Starmer’s human‑rights legal career (Doughty Street Chambers head; authored leading human‑rights texts; Bar Council pro bono award for death‑penalty work in the Caribbean and East Africa; human‑rights adviser to the Northern Ireland Policing Board). 
- Trust: TRUSTED
- Reasoning: Academic institution profile with specific, verifiable career facts. ([seh.ox.ac.uk](https://www.seh.ox.ac.uk/people/keir-starmer?utm_source=openai))

10) URL: Doughty Street Chambers — “Our History”
- Summary: Chambers’ history notes landmark death‑penalty jurisprudence and specifically credits Starmer’s role in extending the Pratt & Morgan death‑row precedent to other jurisdictions—evidence of long‑standing capital‑punishment advocacy. 
- Trust: TRUSTED (with organisational‑source caveat)
- Reasoning: Direct professional context; credible for case‑history and authorship; minor self‑interest acknowledged. ([doughtystreet.co.uk](https://www.doughtystreet.co.uk/index.php/our-history?utm_source=openai))

11) URL: The Independent (2013) — “Human Rights Act must stay, says CPS director Keir Starmer”
- Summary: As outgoing DPP, Starmer argues repealing the Human Rights Act would be a “retrograde step,” emphasising benefits for victims and witnesses; rejects the “villain’s charter” trope. 
- Trust: TRUSTED
- Reasoning: Established outlet; contemporaneous interview anchors a long‑running pro‑HRA position. ([independent.co.uk](https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/human-rights-act-must-stay-says-cps-director-keir-starmer-8877637.html?utm_source=openai))

12) URL: Politics.co.uk (2009) — “Starmer ‘straying into politics’”
- Summary: Reports Starmer’s lecture as DPP defending the Human Rights Act as “basic” and “fundamental”; quotes his argument that losing the HRA would “shame” Britain. 
- Trust: TRUSTED
- Reasoning: Reputable UK politics site; quotes align with other records of the same lecture. ([politics.co.uk](https://www.politics.co.uk/news/2009/10/22/starmer-straying-into-politics/?utm_source=openai))

13) URL: ITV News (1 October 2025) — “PM wants to ‘look again’ at ECHR”
- Summary: Starmer says the government will re‑examine the interpretation (not the existence) of certain ECHR provisions (Articles 3 and 8) in deportation cases; reiterates intent is not to “tear [the ECHR] down.” 
- Trust: TRUSTED
- Reasoning: Mainstream broadcaster; shows nuance that policy review concerns application/interpretation while maintaining ECHR membership. ([itv.com](https://www.itv.com/news/2025-10-01/pm-wants-to-look-again-at-echr-following-itv-news-investigation?utm_source=openai))

Synthesis and conclusion:
- Words: Multiple official, recent statements from Starmer and his ministers commit the UK to remain in the ECHR and to grounding security policy in “respect for human rights and the rule of law” (Nov 4, 2024; Jan 7, 2025; July 17, 2025). This is unusually explicit and repeated for a sitting PM. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/pm-speech-to-the-interpol-general-assembly-4-november-2024?utm_source=openai))
- Deeds: The government introduced the “Hillsborough Law” (Sept 2025) to strengthen victims’ rights and state accountability (duty of candour, parity of legal representation, offences for misleading the public). That is a concrete rights‑advancing reform consistent with valuing human rights. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/hillsborough-law-to-ensure-truth-never-concealed-by-state-again?utm_source=openai))
- Track record: Before politics, Starmer’s distinguished human‑rights legal career included capital‑punishment appeals and authoring leading human‑rights texts; he publicly defended the Human Rights Act as DPP and since. This long arc of advocacy supports the claim that he values human rights beyond mere rhetoric. ([seh.ox.ac.uk](https://www.seh.ox.ac.uk/people/keir-starmer?utm_source=openai))
- Nuance: As PM he has also argued for revisiting how some ECHR rights are applied in deportation cases (interpreting Articles 3 and 8) while expressly rejecting withdrawal from the ECHR—indicating a balance between enforcement priorities and continued commitment to the human‑rights framework. ([itv.com](https://www.itv.com/news/2025-10-01/pm-wants-to-look-again-at-echr-following-itv-news-investigation?utm_source=openai))

Conclusion: On the totality of authoritative evidence—explicit, repeated commitments to the ECHR and rule of law; introduction of rights‑enhancing legislation; and a long human‑rights legal career—there is strong support for the proposition that Keir Starmer values human rights. The government’s interest in recalibrating certain applications of the ECHR in narrow contexts does not contradict that overarching commitment, given the equally explicit insistence on remaining within and respecting the convention. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/pm-speech-to-the-interpol-general-assembly-4-november-2024?utm_source=openai))
